headings.title: Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology
headings.content: Understanding the human body begins with its two foundational disciplines: anatomy and physiology. **Anatomy** investigates bodily structure, examining the physical architecture, spatial relationships, and gross macroscopic features alongside microscopic cellular components. Conversely, **physiology** explores biological function, detailing how organs, tissues, and biochemical pathways work together to sustain life. In clinical nursing practice across Nigeria, these two sciences remain inseparable. A nurse cannot safely administer a drug without knowing the physiological mechanism of action, nor can they accurately assess a physical injury without mapping its exact anatomical location.

headings.title: Levels of Structural Organization
headings.content:
The human body is hierarchically organized from the microscopic chemical level up to the complex organismal level.

- **Chemical level**: Simplest level involving atoms combining to form molecules like water, proteins, and DNA.
- **Cellular level**: Molecules assemble into organelles inside cells, which are the basic structural and functional units of life.
- **Tissue level**: Groups of similar cells and extracellular matrix work together to perform a specific common function, categorized into epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues.
- **Organ level**: Two or more distinct tissue types combine to perform specialized physiological tasks, such as the stomach or heart.
- **Organ system level**: Multiple organs cooperate closely to achieve a major body function, such as the digestive or cardiovascular system.
- **Organism level**: The highest level representing the complete living human being functioning as a unified whole.

headings.title: Characteristics of Living Human Organisms
headings.content: Every living human body exhibits distinct life processes that differentiate it from inanimate matter. **Metabolism** encompasses all chemical reactions occurring within the body, combining constructive anabolism and destructive catabolism to manage energy. **Responsiveness** reflects the ability to sense internal or external environmental changes and react swiftly, a trait heavily relied upon during neurological assessments. **Movement** spans across voluntary locomotion, propulsion of blood through vessels, and intracellular transport. Growth, differentiation, and reproduction round out these vital traits, ensuring that cellular repair, specialization, and species continuation proceed without interruption.

headings.title: Anatomical Terminology and Body Planes
headings.content:
Accurate clinical documentation requires standard terminology. The **anatomical position** serves as the universal reference point: standing upright, feet flat on the floor, upper limbs at the sides, and palms facing forward. 

To visualize internal structures, healthcare professionals rely on imaginary slice cuts called planes:
- **Sagittal plane**: Divides the body vertically into right and left portions.
- **Frontal (coronal) plane**: Divides the body vertically into anterior and posterior portions.
- **Transverse plane**: Divides the body horizontally into superior and inferior portions.

Directional terms such as *anterior*, *posterior*, *proximal*, and *distal* allow nurses to precisely describe wound locations or pain radiation during shift handovers.

headings.title: Body Cavities and Membranes
headings.content:
Internal organs are housed within protective enclosed spaces known as body cavities. The primary division separates the **dorsal body cavity**—containing the cranial cavity and vertebral canal—from the expansive **ventral body cavity**. The ventral cavity is further subdivided by the muscular diaphragm into the superior **thoracic cavity** and the inferior **abdominopelvic cavity**. 

To prevent friction between moving organs and cavity walls, delicate double-layered serous membranes line these regions. The inner layer directly touching the organ is the **visceral layer**, while the outer layer attached to the cavity wall is the **parietal layer**, separated only by a lubricating serous fluid.

headings.title: Homeostasis and Control Systems
headings.content: Survival depends on maintaining a dynamic equilibrium known as **homeostasis**, where internal variables like core temperature, blood glucose, and pH fluctuate within narrow, safe physiological limits. Regulatory feedback loops drive this process. A **negative feedback loop** counteracts a detected change to bring the variable back toward the set point, as seen in blood pressure regulation or thermoregulation. Conversely, a **positive feedback loop** amplifies the initial stimulus rather than reversing it, pushing the system temporarily away from baseline until a specific event concludes, such as blood clotting or uterine contractions during childbirth. When control mechanisms fail, disease or physiological dysfunction ensues.
